messages.text:
Install Graphify locally,

Then we need to plan out how to edit your instruction files and or create skills to turn you into a true full stack developer with critical thinking and real analytical skills.

We also need to set up a harness for you and Claude Code to better interact with the codebase and anything else you need to connect to.

Skills read. Now installing Graphify in my sandbox to validate the toolchain and capture the exact command surface.

Graphify is installed and validated in my sandbox. Here's the full picture, then the plan.

## Install status

**My container (done):** `pip install graphifyy` → v0.8.37, smoke-tested on a mixed Python/Rust corpus. AST extraction, clustering, and the query layer (`graphify explain`, `graphify path`) all work — typed edges with EXTRACTED/INFERRED provenance tags and confidence scores, which maps cleanly onto your q-atom provenance discipline. Zero LLM tokens for code-only extraction. Caveat: my container resets every conversation, so this install is proof-of-toolchain, not infrastructure. The fix is in the harness plan below.

**Your machine (3 commands, ~2 min):**
```
uv tool install graphifyy
cd [redacted:local-path]
graphify update . && graphify install --project && graphify claude install && graphify hook install
```
Three traps I pulled from the docs and release notes: the PyPI package is graphifyy (double-y) — other graphify* packages are unaffiliated, so don't typo it into a squatted package. Plain pip on Windows hits an interpreter-path mismatch where the skill resolves a different Python than where pip installed, causing ModuleNotFoundError — uv tool install or pipx avoid this entirely. And graph rebuilds are CPU-intensive — without guards, concurrent rebuilds pile up (observed: 3 processes at 65–73% CPU, load average 12+, RAM saturated) — so we use the post-commit hook path, **not** `graphify watch`, and given your OneDrive-sync MCP history I'd keep `graphify-out/` excluded from sync.

## The honest coverage analysis

The bundled grammars cover Rust, C#, C++, Python, TypeScript, Go, and ~20 others. **No Odin.** So: Apocrypha, CSSLv3 (~170 Rust crates), OmniMind, and Infinite Labyrinth get full free AST graphs. LoA v10 and the Odin-based CSLv3 parser are invisible to the code path. Your `.csl` spec corpus also isn't code-parsed — docs and PDFs require an LLM call; code-only corpora need no key, so spec extraction is a deliberate, costed one-shot via `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, not something hooks should trigger. My call: ship v1 on code-only for Apocrypha + CSSLv3, run one deliberate doc-extraction pass over the Apocrypha spec suite once the code graphs prove out, and accept Odin blindness for now. Also flagging: the 71.5× token-reduction claim comes from the project's own curated example runs — architecturally plausible, but treat the magnitude as marketing until we measure it on your repos.

## What "editing my instruction files" actually means

Straight answer: my claude.ai system prompt isn't editable. The real control surfaces are four — **user preferences** (small global directives), **memory edits** (30 slots, durable facts), **styles** (tone only, skip), and **user skills** — uploadable packages that land in my environment and trigger contextually. Skills are the only surface with real depth: SKILL.md plus bundled scripts and reference docs, progressive loading, and I have the full authoring/packaging toolchain in this sandbox to build them. On the Claude Code side the surfaces are richer: per-repo and global `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/`, hooks in settings.json for *deterministic* enforcement, subagents, and `.mcp.json`. Graphify already exploits this — one command installs a CLAUDE.md directive plus a PreToolUse hook so Claude consults the knowledge graph before every file-search call, not after.

One thing I'll say plainly because you'd rather stress-test than be sold: skills don't add capability to the underlying model. They change defaults, what context loads, and what discipline gets *enforced*. "Critical thinking" as a skill means encoding your existing epistemics culture — falsification ladder, provenance tags, m₂-style confidence — as a protocol I'm procedurally forced through rather than one I apply when I remember to. That's genuinely valuable (it kills skipped-verification failures), and it's also the ceiling.

## The harness architecture

The keystone is that **graphify-out/ is one artifact with two consumers**. Claude Code queries it live via hooks and CLI. I can't exec on your machine, but Filesystem MCP reads `GRAPH_REPORT.md` and `graph.json` directly — and `copy_file_user_to_claude` exists, so I can pull `graph.json` into my container, one 15-second `pip install`, and run the full query toolchain locally against your real graphs. Both of us reasoning over the same provenance-tagged structure instead of cold-reading files. Later, `graphify merge-graphs` fuses per-repo graphs into a single portfolio graph — given how interconnected Apocrypha/3MNEME/CSSLv3 are, that cross-repo map is probably the highest-leverage artifact of the whole exercise. (Down the road it's also an obvious sixth retrieval channel for 3MNEME, but that's post-v1; not scope-creeping it now.)

Container persistence problem solved the boring way: a `bootstrap/container-setup.sh` in the harness repo that any session of mine runs in one paste.

**Proposed structure** — `[redacted:local-path]`: `skills/` as single source of truth (each skill packages to a `.skill` for claude.ai upload *and* copies into `~/.claude/skills` for Claude Code — write once, install twice), `bootstrap/`, a global `CLAUDE.md` template with the repo map and PRIME DIRECTIVE pointer, and a `DECISIONS.md` ledger.

**v1 skill set, three and only three:** `codebase-onboarding` (session-start protocol: GRAPH_REPORT → INDEX/CLAUDE.md → recent decisions → state my model of the repo *before* touching anything), `critical-analysis` (claim → cited evidence → strongest-counterexample hunt → confidence + what would falsify it — your ladder, enforced), and `fullstack-review` (layered pass: schema → contract → state → UI → tests → rollback, tuned to your actual stacks). Anything beyond three dilutes triggering. I'll author, test, and package them here; you upload and drop folders.

## Sequencing

Phase 0 is yours, one terminal trip: `mkdir _HARNESS` (create_directory still hangs on my end, per standing pattern — and the VIVARIUM mkdir from last session is still pending, same trip), plus `uv tool install graphifyy`. Phase 1: first graphs on Apocrypha and CSSLv3, hooks installed — you or Claude Code, commands above. Phase 2: I write the harness repo contents and the three skills to disk via Filesystem MCP and we iterate with real test prompts. Phase 3: merged portfolio graph + the one-shot CSL doc extraction.

Decisions I've made under standing authority: uv over pip, hooks over watch, Apocrypha+CSSLv3 first, Odin deferred, doc-extraction deferred, three skills not ten. Flag any of those if they hit something I can't see. Otherwise the only blockers are the two mkdirs and the install — say the word once they're done and I'll start writing `codebase-onboarding`, since it's the one the other two depend on.

I need you to think and reason in canonical CSL (do not be lazy about this) for token savings, and speak to me in plain language.

I've given you full filesystem access, please install Graphifyy and make the other changes/improvements to settings, instructions, or whatever you can to make sure you are analyzing problems and data logically and completely, no assumptions or relying on memory when the task is critical and an actual check/lookup/test would be more efficient long-term, etc.

Both servers point at your machine — capital-F has full `[redacted:local-path]`/`[redacted:local-path]` scope, so that's canon from here. Now verifying actual state instead of assuming it: repo root contents and whether my container install survived.

All directories created clean. Updating the standing pattern in memory since it's now stale, then writing the actual content:

Source of truth is your disk, so the packages get built from byte-identical copies of it:

Both validated; packager writes to cwd which was read-only. Rerunning from writable ground:

Done. Reasoning's been in CSL since your message — here's the plain-language state of the world.

**What's now on your disk** — `_HARNESS` exists at the repos root with `CLAUDE.md` (harness conventions + install targets), `DECISIONS.md` (nine entries covering every call I made today, each with its rejected alternative and falsifier), `bootstrap/bootstrap_graphify.ps1`, and `skills/` holding `critical-analysis` and `codebase-onboarding` as source of truth. Structure verified by listing, not assumed.

**What's in my memory** — three new edits: the verify-don't-assume protocol itself (checkable premises get checked; memory is a hint, not evidence; state what was verified vs. inferred), the Graphify operational facts, and a correction to a stale standing pattern — because the protocol paid out within minutes of you issuing it. `create_directory` no longer hangs like it did in May, but it also doesn't create nested paths *despite its own documentation claiming it does*. Live probe beat both my memory and the docs in the same call. That incident is now encoded as an example inside the critical-analysis skill.

**The two skills** — `critical-analysis` is your directive as enforced procedure: every load-bearing premise tagged VERIFIED / INFERRED / REPORTED / ASSUMED, a conversion table mapping claim-types to the actual cheap check, a mandatory counterexample pass, and confidence that must ship with a falsifier or it's dogma. `codebase-onboarding` is the session-start protocol: graph before raw source, ledger tails before whole files, and a stated model of the repo — uncertainties tagged — before any edit. Both are plain-primary with a CSL annex, deliberately, so they execute correctly even in a context that hasn't loaded your notation. The `.skill` files above are packaged from byte-identical copies of what's on your disk — upload those in Settings → Capabilities and I get them here; copy the folders into `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\skills\` and Claude Code gets them too.

**Graphify** — installed and persistent in my container for this session's work. For your machine I wrote the bootstrap script rather than hand-replicating the install, and that's a correctness constraint, not laziness: I read the installer source, and `graphify hook install` embeds the live interpreter path into the git hooks at install time — a value that can only be resolved by execution on your box. Everything hand-replicable, I hand-replicated. The script covers Apocrypha, CSSLv3, and 3MNEME: package install via uv, first AST-only graph build, project-scoped skill, Claude Code wiring, git hooks. It logs to `bootstrap/last_run.log` so I can read the transcript afterward and verify rather than trust.

Two actions on you: run `_HARNESS\bootstrap\bootstrap_graphify.ps1`, and upload the two `.skill` files. Once the script's run, I'll read the log and the three GRAPH_REPORTs, and the next build cycle is the `fullstack-review` skill plus the one-shot doc-path extraction over the Apocrypha spec corpus.
Ran it and saved the skills.

Both skills are live in my environment — confirmed mounted, not assumed. Now verifying the bootstrap actually did what it claims, from the transcript:

The transcript tells a different story than "ran" — good thing we check. Reading the tail to confirm, then the repo state:

Status, verified at both ends:

**Skills: done.** Both `critical-analysis` and `codebase-onboarding` are mounted live in my environment — I listed the mount rather than taking the upload at face value. That half is fully operational as of now.

**Bootstrap: ran, but produced nothing.** The transcript shows exactly what happened: your machine has neither `uv` nor `pipx`, so the script took the pip fallback, pip installed to `AppData\Roaming\Python\Python314\Scripts` which isn't on PATH, and my guard killed the run before any graphs were built or hooks wired. I confirmed independently — no `graphify-out/` in Apocrypha. The guard did its job (better no install than git hooks pointing at an unreachable CLI), but the remedy it printed was useless, and a bootstrap script that can't bootstrap its own dependency was a design miss on my part.

**The script is now v2 on your disk, self-healing.** One behavior change you should know about before running it: when `uv` is absent it now fetches and executes the official installer from astral.sh — a remote script execution, visible in the source and the transcript, but I'm flagging it rather than letting it surprise you. Beyond that it dedupes the stray pip install from the first run, refreshes PATH in-session so it doesn't need a new terminal, resolves the CLI through uv's shim directly if PATH is still stale, and persists uv's bin dir for future shells. Both the failure and the fix are in the DECISIONS ledger with falsifiers.

Same command, one more time: `_HARNESS\bootstrap\bootstrap_graphify.ps1`. Heads up that the CSSLv3 pass will be the slow one — ~170 crates through first-time AST extraction is real work, so let it grind. When it's done I'll read the log and the three graph reports and tell you what your portfolio actually looks like as a graph.
Check again.

Full picture, everything below verified against disk, log, or source — nothing recalled:

**Healthy: CSSLv3 and 3MNEME.** CSSLv3 came out as the highest-fidelity graph of the three — 2,208 files, 55,447 nodes, 115,812 edges at 99% direct extraction, anchored to commit `4e23b5a9`. Its god nodes are exactly what the compiler's core *should* be: `lower_one()`, `envelope()`, `Value`, `EngineState`, `MirType`, `ValueId`, `BodyLowerCtx` — the MIR lowering spine. One detail I genuinely like: your DECISIONS log is the **#2 most-connected node in the entire compiler graph** at 179 edges. The ledger culture is structurally load-bearing, not decorative — the graph just proved it. (No graph.html there; it auto-skips visualization past ~5k nodes. Expected.) 3MNEME is small and clean — 356 nodes, 100% extracted — and its god nodes confirm the implementation now *exists* beyond the specs: `LocalStore`, `MnemeClient`, `BrokerClient`, `SupabaseRemote`, a live TS client and broker with JWT plumbing, matching the May stack-lock.

**Sick: Apocrypha, two findings, one root deeper than the other.** The 22k-node graph is polluted — top god nodes are `__mmask8`, `__m256i`, `__m512i`, vendored SIMD intrinsics. I traced it in graphify's source rather than guessing: the built-in skip list catches `venv`, `.venv`, `*_venv`, `*_env` — and your `.venv-ft` slips all four patterns. Hyphen beats heuristic. I've already written `.graphifyignore` to the repo root covering `.venv*/` plus `.benchmarks/`, `logs/`, `state/`. The rebuild needs `--force` (graphify refuses shrinking rebuilds without it — and this one will shrink a lot, which is the point).

The deeper finding: **Apocrypha has no `.git`.** Verified directly, and it explains the missing freshness section, the blank hook install (a silent no-op — nowhere for post-commit hooks to live), and it means ~1.6 million words of your flagship project are unversioned. That's outside today's scope but it's the kind of thing a tech lead doesn't walk past: my strong recommendation is `git init` + initial commit before the rebuild, which also lets the hooks land properly. Your call on timing.

One command on your end, from inside Apocrypha — `graphify update . --force` (ideally after `git init` + commit, then re-run `graphify hook install` too). Falsifier's already in the ledger: if the rebuilt god nodes aren't Apocrypha-domain symbols — CfC, FHRR, the quantum substrate — something's still leaking and I dig again.
Please give me a prompt for the coding agent to do all of this for me.

Here's the prompt — self-contained, since the agent won't have this session's context. Per standing rule it stays in chat, not on disk.

```
TASK: Repair Apocrypha's version control and rebuild its knowledge graph clean.
Repo: [redacted:local-path]
Work from the repo root. Verify each phase before starting the next. Do not
use any destructive git operations; the only --force in this task is a
graphify rebuild flag, not a git flag.

CONTEXT (already done, do not redo):
- graphify (CLI from PyPI pkg graphifyy, installed via uv) is on PATH.
- .claude/ wiring (skills, settings.json PreToolUse hook, CLAUDE.md
  registration) already exists in this repo.
- A .graphifyignore already exists at repo root excluding .venv*/, venv*/,
  .benchmarks/, logs/, state/. Do not modify it.
- Known defect being fixed: the previous graph build indexed .venv-ft
  (hyphenated venv escapes graphify's built-in skip heuristics), so god
  nodes were vendored SIMD intrinsics (__m256i etc.). Also: this repo has
  never been a git repo, so `graphify hook install` previously no-op'd.

PHASE 0 — Preconditions
- Confirm `git config user.name` and `git config user.email` resolve. If
  either is empty, STOP and report; do not invent an identity.
- Confirm `graphify --version` runs.
- Confirm no .git directory exists. If one exists, skip Phase 1's init but
  still run its .gitignore audit.

PHASE 1 — Version control (order matters: ignore rules BEFORE first add)
- Read the existing .gitignore. Extend it (append, never overwrite) so that
  at minimum these are ignored: .venv/, .venv-ft/, .venv*/, __pycache__/,
  .pytest_cache/, .mypy_cache/, .ruff_cache/, .benchmarks/, logs/, state/,
  graphify-out/cache/, graphify-out/graph.html. Do NOT ignore
  graphify-out/graph.json or graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md — those are
  designed to be committed (union merge driver handles conflicts).
- git init
- git add -A, then BEFORE committing run `git status --short | head -50`
  and sanity-check: no .venv or .venv-ft paths staged. If any appear, fix
  .gitignore and re-stage. 
- Commit: "Initial commit: Apocrypha under version control (929-file corpus)"
- Verify: `git rev-parse HEAD` returns a hash.

PHASE 2 — Hooks (now that a git repo exists)
- Run: graphify hook install
- Verify .git/hooks/post-commit and post-checkout exist and reference
  graphify. Note: future commits trigger incremental AST-only rebuilds;
  that is intended.

PHASE 3 — Clean rebuild
- Run: graphify update . --force
  (--force is required and expected: the node count will DROP sharply
  because the venv pollution is being excluded. That shrink is the goal.)
- Read graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md. Extract: file count, node/edge/
  community counts, extraction percentages, and the God Nodes list.

PHASE 4 — Falsifier check (do not skip)
- PASS condition: top god nodes are Apocrypha domain symbols (expect names
  related to CfC, FHRR, hypervectors, predictive coding, model_from_cfg,
  cssl modules, daemons, etc.).
- FAIL condition: any god node matching __m*, _mm*, __mmask*, v128_t,
  __DEVICE__, or other vendor-header intrinsics. On FAIL: report which
  paths leaked (graphify explain "<node>" shows source files) and STOP.

PHASE 5 — Commit the graph + ledger
- git add graphify-out/graph.json graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md .gitignore
  .graphifyignore && commit: "Clean knowledge graph post venv-exclusion fix"
  (The post-commit hook will fire an incremental rebuild; with no code
  changes it is a near-no-op. Expected, ignore it.)
- Append one line to [redacted:local-path] and
  one to [redacted:local-path] format:
  DATE | DECISION | STRONGEST REJECTED ALTERNATIVE | FALSIFIER
  recording: git init + clean graph rebuild, the alternative (staying
  unversioned / keeping polluted graph), and the falsifier (god nodes
  regress to intrinsics on future rebuilds => exclusion rules broke).

REPORT BACK, tagged per claim: what you VERIFIED (commands + outputs),
old vs new node counts, the new top-10 god nodes, and anything ASSUMED.
```

One judgment call encoded in there worth flagging: I have the agent committing `graph.json` and the report but ignoring `graph.html` and the cache — that follows graphify's own design (the merge driver exists precisely so graph.json can live in git), and it keeps your first-ever Apocrypha commit from hauling rendering artifacts. When the agent reports back, paste me the god-node list — that's the falsifier, and I want to eyeball it against what the substrate's core *should* look like before we call Phase 3 of the harness (community labeling and the merged portfolio graph) ready.

All five phases complete. Apocrypha is now under version control with a clean knowledge graph, working tree clean, and the falsifier check passed.
VERIFIED (command → output)
Phase 0 — Preconditions
git config user.name / user.email → Apocky / [redacted:email]
graphify --version → graphify 0.8.37 (one wrinkle: not on this shell's PATH; resolved at ~\.local\bin\graphify.exe, PATH prepended per command)

graphify hook install → both .git/hooks/post-commit and post-checkout exist, reference graphify, and pin the interpreter at ...\uv\tools\graphifyy\Scripts\python.exe. Observed working live: the ledger commit fired a background rebuild that correctly no-op'd ("No code-graph topology changes detected"), and graph-only commits were skipped by the hook's loop guard.
Phase 3/4 — Clean rebuild + falsifier

nodes	22,143	5,817

New top-10: Registry (234), Codebook (222), ProvenanceSource (177), Provenance (175), ToolResult (163), Executor (158), Hv (153), EpisodicStore (145), PermissionTier (142), ToolArgs (140) — all Apocrypha domain symbols. PASS.
Regex sweep of the entire graph.json for __m256|__m128|__m512|_mm_|_mm256|_mm512|__mmask|v128_t|__DEVICE__ → 0 hits. The two literal .venv string matches are a docstring in tests/benchmark_apocrypha.py quoting a run command — text, not indexed venv content.
Phase 5 — Commits + ledgers

Pipe-format decision line appended to both DECISIONS.md and _HARNESS\DECISIONS.md, with the falsifier (god nodes regress to intrinsics ⇒ exclusion rules broke).
Follow-up commits: df00c0a (ledger), d89f0b4 (graph metadata — the force rebuild had also purged ~720 stale venv-node labels from tracked manifest.json/.graphify_labels.json, which the prescribed git add list missed), 8d64c05 (HANDOFF_v0.csl session block per project handoff discipline). git status is clean.
ASSUMED
The "929-file corpus" wording in the initial commit message refers to the old graph's corpus count (929 files indexed pre-fix), not git-tracked files (468) — used verbatim as prescribed.
The extraction shift (84%→57% extracted) is expected, not a regression: vendored C headers extract near-perfectly via AST and were inflating the old percentage; the 43% INFERRED edges (avg confidence 0.55) could be raised later with semantic extraction (GEMINI_API_KEY), noted in the handoff GAPS.

Good report — and properly tagged, which means the discipline propagated to the agent. Per protocol, your report is REPORTED until I've spot-checked it independently. Three probes:

Everything checks out. The verdict, with what I verified versus what I'm reading into it:

**Verified independently:** `.git` exists with live hooks, the rebuilt report matches your agent's numbers byte-for-byte — 329 files, 5,817 nodes, 14,152 edges, 273 communities, anchored at `04fb069f` — and the god-node list is identical. The agent's report is fully upgraded from REPORTED to VERIFIED, including its catch of my miss: the prescribed `git add` list in my prompt didn't account for the force-rebuild purging ~720 stale venv labels from `manifest.json`. It handled that correctly without instruction, which is the behavior the prompt's tagging discipline was supposed to produce. Both ledgers carry the resolution.

**The reading that matters.** Look at what floated to the top once the vendor noise left: `Provenance` and `ProvenanceSource` are #3 and #4 most-connected abstractions in the entire codebase, `PermissionTier` is #9, `Hv` and `EpisodicStore` hold #7 and #8, `Registry`/`Codebook` lead. The brutal truth is that the jail solves security but *complicates* the UI, because the validated execution path is now `bubblewrap-inside-WSL2` — a Linux subprocess wrapped in a kernel cage. A Windows-native GUI can't just shell out to it; the UI has to drive a process that lives across the WSL boundary, inside a jail that rebuilds per invocation. That's the central design constraint, and it kills the simplest options.

What remains, in dependency order:

**1. Decide the UI's relationship to the jail — this is the architecture fork, and nothing else can start until it's settled.** Three shapes: **(a)** the UI runs *inside* WSL too (a local web server in the distro, you hit it from a Windows browser) — cleanest, because the UI and the jailed agent share a filesystem and OS; **(b)** the UI runs on Windows and talks to a thin daemon inside WSL over a socket — more moving parts, a protocol to define; **(c)** skip the bespoke UI and use an existing ACP-compatible editor. That last one is the sleeper: I verified earlier that Kimi speaks the Agent Client Protocol so Zed and JetBrains can drive it — I do *not* know whether CodeWhale speaks ACP or any editor protocol, and that single unknown could collapse most of this work into "point Zed at it." **2. Confirm CodeWhale's actual programmatic surface.** The kickoff *assumed* "runtime APIs." I have not verified that's real — whether CodeWhale exposes a stable headless/streaming interface a UI can drive (the `--output-format stream-json` in the jail script is a promising hint), or an ACP/LSP server mode, or nothing but the TUI. The entire UI plan rests on this and it's currently REPORTED-at-best. This is the first thing to nail down.

**3. The cost/trace ledger (M1) is a UI prerequisite, not a parallel track.** A cockpit's whole value is showing plan / diff / approval / cost at a glance. Those are exactly the M1 artifacts. Building UI before M1 means building a dashboard with nothing to display. So M1 comes first regardless.

**4. The approval-gate tension.** Your security model *requires* a human on the gate for non-throwaway work (that's the whole finding). A UI that runs `--auto` for smoothness re-opens the hole. So the UI's core interaction *is* the approval surface — render the pending action, the diff, the target path, and an allow/deny — which is more valuable than a chat box anyway, but it means the UI is fundamentally an approval-and-trace viewer first, a chat second.

**5. The panels themselves** (the easy part, last): session view, diff/approval pane, cost meter, the graphify `graph.html` embed, the wiki browser. This is ordinary frontend work once 1–4 are settled, and your cssl.dev / Next.js experience covers it.

That's a genuinely sharp instinct, and it cuts in two directions — one real win, one trap that would burn the whole experiment if we didn't catch it. Let me reason through it properly before you commit the agent to it.

**Where you're right.** The CSL annexes in our skills already prove the compression is real — the `critical-analysis` skill carries its whole five-stage protocol in maybe 60 tokens of dense notation. If the binding constraint is *prompt token budget*, CSL is the highest-density encoding you have. So at first glance, writing Kimi's lean agent prompt in CSL means you could fit *more actual instruction* under the 2k ceiling, or hit the ceiling with room to spare. That part is sound.

**Where it's a trap, and it's the load-bearing point.** The whole reason Lever 1 exists is that Gemma-12B is **weak** — not just token-limited, but limited in *reasoning capacity per token*. CSL is dense precisely because it offloads work onto the reader: every glyph like `⊢` or `W!` or `Σ:` is a pointer the reader has to *decompress* from prior fluency. You and I read CSL natively. A frozen 12B with no CSL in its training distribution does not — it would burn its scarce reasoning budget trying to parse the notation instead of spending it on the actual task. You'd be trading a token-count problem for a comprehension problem, and comprehension is the exact axis Gemma is worst on. The practitioner finding that fixed weak tool-callers wasn't "compress the prompt" — it was structured tool guidance as tables, not paragraphs, plus a small tool surface. Tables are *low* cognitive load: explicit, positional, nothing to decode. CSL is the opposite — minimal tokens, *maximal* decode load. For a weak model those are opposite directions even though both look like "make it shorter."

So the honest answer is: **CSL would likely make Lever 1 worse, not better, for Gemma specifically** — and the failure would be silent and confusing, looking like "the model's just dumb" rather than "we handed it notation it can't parse."

But — and this is why your instinct isn't wrong, just mis-targeted — there are three places the idea is genuinely good, and they're worth capturing rather than discarding:

The token budget isn't actually the constraint that's hurting you. Gemma serves at 32k context; Kimi's default prompt is ~11k. The problem was never that 11k *didn't fit* — it's that 11k of *tool-decision surface* overwhelmed Gemma's ability to act coherently. Shrinking to 2k matters because it shrinks the *decision space*, not because it saves context room. So optimizing for raw token-count via CSL is solving a constraint that isn't the binding one. The binding one is cognitive load, and CSL raises it.

Where CSL *does* belong: it's the right encoding the moment the model is strong enough to read it. If Lever 2 lands a stronger local coder, or if you run the GUI on a cloud model (DeepSeek, K2.7 — trillion-param, far more likely to handle dense notation), then a CSL agent prompt becomes a real efficiency play, because now the reader can actually decompress it. And it's already the right encoding for the **inter-agent** layer — when *Claude Code or I* hand work to the coding agent, CSL handoffs are pure win because the readers are CSL-fluent. The principle holds; it's just gated on reader capability.

So my recommendation: **don't write Gemma's prompt in CSL — but make it an explicit variable in the experiment**, because we shouldn't assume, we should measure. The cleanest version tests both encodings against the same weak model and lets the tool_results settle it, rather than me asserting "CSL will lose" from theory. If I'm wrong and Gemma parses a CSL prompt fine, that's a discovery worth having; if I'm right, we've proven it cheaply instead of guessing.

The word you're reaching for is right, and it points at exactly the mechanism — but I want to make sure we land on the *real* biological answer and not the seductive-but-wrong version of it, because the difference determines whether Lever 1 actually improves or just gets a prettier prompt.

**How the reflex actually forms — and the part people get wrong.** The tempting story is "practice compiles deliberation into reflex," and that's half true but misleading. The deeper mechanism is **chunking and proceduralization**: a novice represents a task as many small explicit decisions, each consuming working memory; an expert has *collapsed* clusters of those decisions into single units that fire as one. The chess master doesn't evaluate twenty moves faster than you — they perceive the board as a few meaningful chunks instead of thirty-two pieces, so there are fewer decisions to make at all. The London-cab-driver, the touch-typist, the fluent reader: in every case skill is *reduction of the number of choice-points*, not acceleration of choosing. The decision didn't get faster. The decision **stopped being a decision** — it got absorbed into perception or into a pre-bound routine.

And critically: this happens in two different places in the brain, and only one of them is available to us. Humans and animals proceduralize by literally *moving* the computation — from prefrontal deliberative circuits to the basal ganglia and cerebellum, structures that execute learned routines with almost no central oversight. That migration requires **changing the substrate through repetition**. A frozen model cannot do that. Its weights don't update from your repo sessions. So the one mechanism that *defines* biological reflex — rewiring through practice — is exactly the one we don't have access to with Gemma. I want that stated plainly because it's the trap: we cannot make Gemma *learn* reflexes, so any plan that depends on "it'll get better with use" is dead on arrival for a frozen model. (It's *alive* for Apocrypha — that's literally Apocrypha's whole thesis, interaction-time learning, reflexes forming in the substrate. Different track, real answer there. Not here.)

**So how do small-brained animals do it without big deliberation?** They mostly *don't deliberate at all* — they run **fixed action patterns**: hardwired stimulus→response routines where a specific releaser triggers a complete behavior with no decision in between. A digger wasp's entire nest-provisioning sequence is a chain of these. The "intelligence" isn't in the wasp's runtime reasoning; it's *pre-compiled into the trigger structure* by evolution. The animal is coherent not because it chose well but because **its environment only presents it with cues that map cleanly to a small, fixed repertoire of responses.** That is the mechanism we can actually steal, because it doesn't require the agent to learn — it requires *us* to do the compilation in advance and shape the environment so the few cues map unambiguously to few responses.

That reframes Lever 1 completely. We've been treating the lean agent as "a smaller prompt." It isn't. **It's us doing the proceduralization that Gemma can't do for itself — pre-chunking the work so that at every step the model faces a fixed-action-pattern-sized decision instead of an open one.** The lean prompt and the small tool set aren't compression; they're *externalized expertise*. We are being Gemma's evolution and Gemma's basal ganglia, baking the chunks in from outside because the model can't bake them in from within.

Here's how that principle turns into concrete Lever 1 improvements — each one is "remove a choice-point," which is the only lever that actually matters:

**1. Collapse the decision *tree*, not just the tool *count*.** The real killer isn't fifteen tools — it's that at each turn Gemma faces the full cross-product of "which tool × which arguments × is the task done yet." Reduce the *branching*, not just the leaves. The strongest form: a **forced workflow** where the agent's available actions change by phase. In an "edit" task the only tools that exist are ReadFile→StrReplaceFile→done; the model literally cannot see SearchWeb because in this phase it isn't offered. Kimi's plan-mode/agent-file machinery may let you gate tools per-phase — if so, that's the single highest-leverage change, because it turns an open decision into a near-deterministic sequence. That's the digger wasp: the next action is structurally constrained, so "choosing" collapses toward "proceeding."

**2. Make the cue→response mapping unambiguous (kill the near-synonyms).** Gemma hallucinated tools partly because the tool set contained overlapping options — WriteFile vs StrReplaceFile vs Shell-with-cat-redirect can all "change a file," so the model dithers or invents. A fixed-action-pattern works because *one* releaser maps to *one* response. So: expose exactly one tool per *intent*. One way to edit. One way to read. No two tools whose descriptions could both answer the same task, because every overlap is a choice-point you're paying for in coherence.

**3. Put the cognition *behind* the tool, so the model's decision stays trivial** (this is the Rung-2 insight from last turn, now properly grounded). Don't give Gemma a graph-query tool *and* a file-read tool *and* a search tool and make it orchestrate them. Give it a tool whose *name is the intent* — `find_implementation` — that internally does the graphify query, the ranking, the file resolution, and hands back the answer. The richness lives in the deterministic script; the model's choice is reduced to "is this a find-implementation situation? yes → call it." We are doing the orchestration-reasoning *for* it, in code, in advance. Maximum cognition, minimum decision surface. This is the resolution of the apparent paradox from last turn — "more cognitive tools floods the weak channel" — you don't add tools, you add *depth behind a fixed number of tools*.

**4. Constrain the output shape so format isn't a decision.** Part of a weak model's budget goes to *how to phrase the tool call*. Pin it: structured output / grammar-constrained decoding via llama.cpp's GBNF if Kimi's serving path allows it, so the model physically cannot emit a malformed tool_call — the grammar makes the valid shape the *only* shape. That's not a prompt change; it's removing format-choice from the model entirely by enforcing it at the sampler. If the serving stack supports it, it's possibly the most reliable single fix, because it makes an entire class of failure impossible rather than discouraged.

**5. The table-vs-CSL question from before, now answered by the mechanism.** The structured table wins *for the cue-mapping layer* precisely because a table is a lookup, not a parse — it's the lowest-decode-load way to present "this cue → this response," which is what a fixed-action-pattern needs. CSL loses *here* not because it's dense but because it asks the model to *decode before deciding*, adding a step. (CSL wins where the *reader is fluent* — i.e. the stronger-model and inter-agent layers, unchanged from last turn.) So the mechanism actually adjudicates the A/B we were going to run empirically: tables for the reflex layer, because reflexes are lookups.

The through-line: **we cannot give Gemma reflexes, but we can build an environment where it doesn't need them** — where the work has been pre-chunked, the cues are unambiguous, the cognition is pre-orchestrated behind intent-named tools, and the output shape is enforced rather than chosen. Every one of those is *us* doing the proceduralization externally that a human brain does internally through practice. That's not a workaround for a weak model; it might be the *correct* architecture for *any* frozen model, and it's the same philosophy as your whole substrate — intelligence in the structure, the model as one constrained organ.

That analogy is exactly right and it's worth pausing on, because it diagnoses the whole thing: multiple-choice converts *recall* into *recognition*, and recognition is cheap where recall is expensive. That's precisely what phase-gating tools does — it turns "what should I do?" (open recall over the whole tool space) into "which of these two?" (recognition among the offered options). You've found the mechanism's name. Good.

Now your actual proposal — the key/index plus dense decision trees, paying tokens upfront to save them per-decision. Let me reason through it honestly, because half of it is right and half of it walks straight back into the trap we just identified, and the split is subtle.

**First, the amortization premise itself.** "Higher upfront, lower per-chain" only pays off if the upfront cost is paid *once* and reused across *many* decisions. With Kimi+Gemma, the system prompt is prefix — it sits at the front of context every turn, and with prefix caching it's processed once and cached. So the *compute* cost of a fat prompt amortizes well. But here's the catch that isn't about tokens at all: the prompt doesn't just cost tokens to *process*, it costs **attention budget to hold**. A weak model attending over a 3k-token dense index every turn is spending its scarce attention on the index, every turn — that cost does *not* amortize, it recurs per decision. So your framing has a hidden conflation: token-processing cost amortizes (good, prefix cache), but cognitive-load cost recurs (bad, and it's the load we're fighting). The exam analogy holds: a multiple-choice exam with a 40-page glossary you must cross-reference for every question is *not* low-load just because the glossary is "paid for once" — you re-pay the lookup cost on every single question.

So the question becomes: which kind of thing are you putting in the upfront index — the kind that genuinely converts to recognition, or the kind that adds a recurring lookup?

**The part of your idea that's right — and it's a real improvement.** A **shorthand key for tools** is good, *if* the shorthand is what the model emits, not what it has to decode. Here's the distinction. If you define `RF = ReadFile, SR = StrReplaceFile, FI = find_implementation` and then ask Gemma to *read* trees written in that shorthand and *expand* them to decide — that's added decode load, the CSL trap again. But if the shorthand is the **output token** — you constrain the model (via grammar) to emit `RF("path")` and a deterministic layer expands `RF`→the real ReadFile call — then you've done something genuinely useful: you've shrunk the *action space the model has to produce* down to a tiny, unambiguous vocabulary. Short, distinct output tokens are *easier* for a weak model to emit correctly than long tool names it can fumble or hallucinate variants of. That's not the CSL trap; that's the opposite — it's reducing output-side decision surface. So: **shorthand as the emitted action vocabulary = win; shorthand as something the model must parse to think = loss.** Same notation, opposite effect, depending on which side of the model it sits.

**The part that walks back into the trap.** "Build the simplified trees in dense notation" — if you mean the *model* navigates a dense decision tree in the prompt, that's exactly the recall-disguised-as-recognition failure. A decision tree the model has to *traverse by reasoning* ("I'm at node 3, condition X, so branch to 3b...") is open reasoning wearing a tree's clothing — it's *more* steps, not fewer, and dense notation makes each step a decode. The exam version: that's not multiple-choice, it's a flowchart you must mentally execute, which is harder than a plain question. The decision tree is powerful — but only if **the runtime executes it, not the model.** If the *scaffolding* holds the tree and uses it to decide which 2-3 tools to even offer the model at this phase, then the tree's branching has been spent in deterministic code and the model just sees "here are your 2 options" — recognition. The tree belongs in the harness, not the prompt.

Here's the synthesis, and it resolves your instinct cleanly: **the decision tree is real and valuable, but it lives in two halves on opposite sides of the model.**

- The **branching logic** (which phase am I in, therefore which tools exist) → executed by the scaffolding, *before* the model is called. The model never traverses it; it just receives the pruned option set. This is the phase-gating from last turn, and it's where your "tree" should live.
- The **action vocabulary** (the short, distinct tokens the model emits) → a shorthand key, grammar-enforced on output, so the model produces `SR(...)` not a hallucinated tool name. This is where your "shorthand" pays off, on the output side.
- What stays in the prompt is **minimal and recognition-shaped**: a tiny table of *only the currently-offered* actions in shorthand, with one-line cue→action mappings. Not the whole tree, not a global index — just "here, now, these two, pick."

So your upfront-cost intuition is right but I'd retarget *what* you spend it on. Don't spend upfront tokens on a fat index the model must hold and consult — spend upfront **engineering effort** (in the harness, once) building the phase-gate tree and the shorthand-expansion layer, so that *per decision* the model sees a tiny recognition problem. The cost you're front-loading isn't tokens-in-the-prompt; it's *our* work compiling the decision structure into the environment. That's the same move as before — externalized proceduralization — just sharpened: the tree is the proceduralized expertise, and it executes in code, handing the model multiple-choice questions one at a time.

The one place a small in-prompt key genuinely earns its tokens: a **stable shorthand legend** for the handful of actions, because that legend converts long fumble-prone tool names into short distinct emittable tokens, and *that* conversion is recognition-friendly and reused every turn. Keep it tiny — five or six entries — and it's pure win. The moment it grows into a reference manual the model must search, it's flipped back into recurring lookup cost.

The deep reason a proof matters here: it is **the one confidence signal you don't have to trust a model for.** Everything else in this composite — the generator's answer, the reranker's relevance score, even Apocrypha's surprise gate — is a probabilistic organ that can be confidently wrong (the MM2 lesson, the whole conversation). A Lean 4 proof is checkable by a *deterministic verifier*, so a proof-carrying output is grounded in a way no model assertion ever is. That makes it the **top of a confidence hierarchy**, and the natural anchor for the precision/affect layer you already specced (33): proven → maximal precision, trust autonomously; empirically-validated → high; retrieved-with-provenance → medium; model-asserted → low, flag for review. "Leveraged right" means the composite *knows which tier each of its outputs sits in* and acts accordingly — which is also I-65 made operational: the system honestly distinguishes what it's *proven* from what it merely *believes*, instead of emitting uniform confidence over both.

The honest limit, stated plainly so it doesn't become magical thinking: **provable correctness only exists in formalizable domains.** Lean proofs cover math and formally-specifiable code properties — type-correctness, invariant-preservation, "this refactor changed nothing observable." Most of what an agent does (natural language, fuzzy judgment, real-world tasks) has no formal spec to prove against, and pretending otherwise would be the demiurge move — declaring a floor that isn't there. So the leverage is *surgical*: identify the subset of the agent's work that **can** be formalized, route only that through a proof-carrying path, and treat the proof as a hard high-confidence flag — while the rest stays probabilistic with calibrated uncertainty. You don't get provable everything. You get provable *where it matters*, and the system that knows the boundary.
